summary: Reviews issues with the cryptographic mechanisms used to protect routing protocols. These mechanisms use a hash digest of the message and a shared key to show it came unaltered from an authorized neighbor router. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routing protocols can attach a keyed digest to messages so neighboring routers can check who sent them and whether they changed in transit. RFC 6039 surveys limitations in these mechanisms, especially manual key management and replay protection.

questions: cryptographic protection of routing protocols issues
what are the problems with routing protocol authentication
why is manual keying a problem for ospf

what is wrong with bfd authentication
subtitle: A survey of management and replay-protection limits in cryptographic methods used by routing protocols.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols use keyed digests to authenticate neighboring routers and detect message changes, but manual keying and protocol details leave management and replay risks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews authentication approaches in OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS, BGP-4, RIP, and BFD, including key management, message coverage, and replay behavior.
tldr.outcome: The document proposes no protocol changes and adds no security requirements. It records limitations of the mechanisms it reviews.

facts.label: Protocols reviewed
facts.value: OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS, BGP-4, RIP, BFD

today: RFC 6039 is Informational and was published in October 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo proposes no protocol changes.

sections.title: What Keyed Digests Protect
sections.content:
The routing protocols discussed in the memo use a digest produced from a message and a shared secret key. A receiving router recomputes the digest to check that the sender is authorized to exchange routing information and that the message was not altered in transit.

These digests do not provide confidentiality. The RFC identifies two broad limitations: manually configuring and changing shared keys is difficult, and some manual-key configurations cannot provide complete replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A keyed digest checks message integrity and possession of a shared key. It does not hide the message, and captured messages may still be replayed in some configurations.

sections.title: Hash Concerns in Context
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes a pre-image attack, which seeks an input for a chosen hash, from a collision attack, which finds two inputs with the same hash. It says documented hash collisions did not present an obvious known attack on routing protocols at the time, partly because many altered field values would make a packet invalid.

The authors note published concerns about MD5 and SHA-1 but distinguish them from keyed MD5 and HMAC-MD5 as used by the protocols. The memo says these attacks were not then applicable to the routing protocols it reviewed, while noting that organizations may prefer SHA-family algorithms for policy reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC discusses weaknesses reported for hash functions but says those findings did not directly create a known attack on the keyed mechanisms it reviewed. It also notes that algorithm choice may follow local policy.

sections.title: OSPF and IS-IS Limitations
sections.content:
OSPFv2 uses manually configured per-link keys and does not negotiate keys or algorithms. Its sequence number resets when an adjacency forms or goes down, and multiple packets can share a sequence number. On broadcast networks, neighbors share a key, and the packet IP header is not covered by the described digest.

OSPFv3 relies on IPsec with manual keys; the RFC cites replay risks in that configuration. IS-IS uses shared keys for link-state information but does not put a sequence number on Hellos. The memo describes replay cases that can reset adjacencies, cause link-state flooding, or increase sequence numbers toward their maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF and IS-IS have replay and key-management limits described in the memo. Some message fields or packet headers are not covered by the authentication mechanism.

sections.title: BGP, RIP, and BFD Limitations
sections.content:
BGP uses TCP and, in the deployments discussed, the TCP MD5 option. The RFC notes that peers often configure shared keys manually and rarely change them. It also describes a period during key changes when some implementations accept packets with bad digests.

RIPv2 authentication does not cover the UDP and IP headers, and replayed packets with altered source addresses can affect routing. BFD uses optional shared-key authentication and a 32-bit sequence number; the memo discusses replay, denial-of-service, and sequence-number wrap-around concerns. It notes that TCP-AO had obsoleted TCP MD5 but was not yet widely used in the deployments it described.
sections.plainLanguage: The remaining protocols have their own limits involving manual keys, replayed messages, or fields that are not authenticated. The details differ by protocol, so the memo reviews them separately.

sections.title: Scope of the Review
sections.content:
RFC 6039 outlines security issues that arise from the manual-key methods used by several routing protocols. It does not propose specific changes to those protocols.

The document also creates no new security requirements. Its purpose is to describe known limitations and possible ways that attackers could exploit them.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a survey of security and management issues. It does not define a replacement authentication method or change protocol requirements.
